n: The heading ties this psalm to David’s wars with the Arameans and Edom. It opens with national lament: a defeat has made it feel as though God rejected his people. They plead, “Turn back to us.”
The defeat is pictured as an earthquake that split the land. They ask God to repair its cracks.
God has given his people hard times, like a drink of wine that makes them stagger.

f.g: Wine that makes one reel — a picture of confusion and judgment.

n: Yet God has given a banner to his faithful as a rallying point. A banner marked where troops should gather in battle.

f.g: A standard or flag for rallying troops.

n: So that God’s beloved people may be saved, the psalmist asks God to rescue with his right hand. Verses 5–12 also appear in Psalm 108.
God has spoken from his holy place, like a triumphant warrior dividing up the land. Shechem and Succoth are sites west and east of the Jordan.

f.g: A city in central Canaan where Abraham and Jacob stopped.
A valley east of the Jordan where Jacob built booths.

n: God claims Israel’s tribes: Gilead and Manasseh in the east, Ephraim as his helmet, and Judah as his royal scepter.

f.g: My helmet — Ephraim was the strongest northern tribe.
My scepter — the royal tribe of David.

n: God speaks with scorn of Israel’s enemies: Moab is his washbasin, he throws his sandal onto Edom (claiming ownership), and he shouts over Philistia.

f.g: A washbasin — a lowly household item.
Tossing a sandal onto land was a gesture of claiming it.

n: Now the king asks: who will lead me into the fortified city of Edom?

f.g: Probably Bozrah or Sela (Petra), Edom’s rocky fortress.

n: Only God can — the same God who seemed to reject them and didn’t go out with their armies.
Human help is useless; only God can rescue from trouble.

f.w: vain is the help of man

n: With God we will act bravely, for he will trample our enemies. The psalm moves from defeat to renewed courage.

f.w: Through God we shall do valiantly
